{"approach":"From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail through the beaver meadows; at the first switchback past the meadows, beyond the Colchuck/Stuart Lake trail fork, leave the trail to the south on an obscure, unmaintained climbers' path, crossing Stuart Lake creek on logs, to reach the base of the northeast-facing couloir below Sherpa Peak. The path is unmaintained and can be hard to follow.","itinerary":"Approach from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to a camp in the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut below the couloir; alpine-start to climb the couloir (snow/ice to roughly 50 degrees) to its top, then scramble up and right to the Balanced Rock summit via a short 5.0 pitch; descend the same route or via Sherpa Pass."}

{"approach":"Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.","approach_variants":[{"baseFinding":"The base is a free-standing pillar, not a face, and that is why this one cannot be mistaken once you are close. From Table Rock a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the range divide, putting you on the crest east of the balanced rock. Follow the crest west over blocks and sandy exposed benches at Class 3-4 until you are standing at the foot of a detached granite pillar. That pillar is the route.

The move at the base is the proof: you cannot simply start climbing. Gaining the pedestal at the bottom needs a shoulder-stand off a partner, or a rope thrown or lassoed over the point of the pedestal. If you have found a start you can climb unaided, you are on the peak's ordinary ridge scrambling and not on this feature.

Second confirmation, and it is unusual for the range: above the pedestal the climbing is bolt-protected friction at about 5.7 to a flat top, with a single ageing bolt up there used to rappel back down. Bolts on Sherpa are rare enough that finding them is strong positive evidence.

Direction check in cloud: you arrive at the crest east of the pillar and walk west to it. If you are heading east along the crest you are walking away from the rock and from Sherpa's true summit, which lies beyond the rock to the west.

And a scope warning worth reading before you commit: this is not a route up the mountain. It is the technical feature near the summit, and most parties combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. If your objective was the peak, the pillar is an add-on rather than the way up.","distMi":6.5,"hazards":["A steep, loose descent off Longs Pass in both directions","An Ingalls Creek ford that is a genuine crossing in early-season snowmelt","Loose rockfall-prone gully and basin terrain — helmets strongly advised","A dry upper basin: no water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction","An exposed Class 3-4 crest traverse to reach the pillar","A single ageing bolt as the rappel anchor off the top","The unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself"],"name":"Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and Table Rock","notes":"From the Esmeralda / Longs Pass trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take Longs Pass Trail #1229 through open pine and sage switchbacks about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft.

Drop off the north side on the steep eroded boot path, losing 1,400-1,600 ft over about a mile to Ingalls Creek at roughly 4,800 ft. Ford the creek — a rock-hop in low water, a real wet crossing in snowmelt — and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail east about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike junction at about 4,700 ft. That junction is the last dependable water before the alpine basin.
